Trt_Concerns_Desc: The objective of the Camp Harney-Cow Creek Ecological Restoration Project is to remove western juniper and other conifers from vegetative communities where conifers are encroaching or have taken over desirable plant communities across the 16,201-acre Project Area. The conifer encroachment has led to losses of desirable vegetative communities, losses of wildlife habitat, degraded stream conditions, reduced productivity, and conditions that threaten the existence and perpetuation of bald eagle winter roost sites. Management action is needed to halt and reverse the impacts of juniper and to a lesser degree other conifer species encroachment.\r\nWith historic grazing practices (which removed fine herbaceous fuels) and the start of fire suppression activities at the turn of the century, the influence of fire in the Project Area was greatly reduced. Fire was the principal factor that controlled conifer encroachment into shrub-grassland communities in the Intermountain West prior to Euro-American immigration (110 to 130 years ago) (West 1999; Miller and Tausch 2001). As the frequency and size of fires across the landscape lessened, juniper expanded into shrub-grassland communities with an overall loss in ecosystem function and a dramatic alteration in historic biodiversity, hydrologic cycles, fauna, and nutrient cycling (Bates et al. 1998).

Treatment_Type: Noxious Weeds: Weed Control - Herbicide Application
Objectives: Apply imazapic to reduce invasive annual grass species, including cheatgrass and medusahead. To prepare the seed bed for aerial seedings in the fall of 2023 (FY24) focusing on cheatgrass control for seedbed preparation for the aerial seeding treatment to enhance germination and seedling establishment of native perennials.
Planned_Implementation: One aerial application of imazapic herbicide to reduce the threat invasive annual grasses (IAGs) pose to general greater sage-grouse habitat and to reduce competition from IAGs for moisture and nutrients required for seedling success following aerial seeding one-year post-imazapic treatment.\r\nThe aerial herbicide application would be applied on 1,105 acres of the burned area. Imazapic would be applied at the appropriate rate per acre and include appropriate adjuvants to target IAGs and other invasive annuals. Treatment effectiveness will determine if additional aerial herbicide treatments will be necessary in the future.
Actual_Implementation: During fall 2022, approximately a 1,056 acre application of imazapic was applies to reduce invasive annual grass species, including cheatgrass and medusahead.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
In 2022, the monitoring for the first year after the fire in the Aerial Seeding area showed 8.4% invasive annual grass cover. The deep-rooted perennial grass cover 10.4% cover, and the shallow-rooted perennial grass cover was 6.4% (Table 7-2). The plots overall had median basal diameter of less than a half inch and a density of 4.25 plants per m2, not including seedlings (Table 7-1).

Aerial Herbicide application for invasive annual grasses was delayed one year due to procurement restrains and was applied during the fall 2022.

In 2023, the monitoring for the second year after fire, one year post treatments, showed 1.1% foliar cover for invasive annual grasses. The reduction of invasive annual grasses was successful the first year after herbicide application. Data shows that deep-rooted perennial grass and shallow-rooted perennial grasses did not increase in foliar cover over the last year. The most notable difference between the two years within the treatment area is the increase in nonnative forb cover. Prickly lettuce increased by 17.5% foliar cover.
